en: Points of Controversy,
Chapter on the Path of Certainty,
Sixth Section.
The Discourse on Dependent Origination:
Is dependent origination unconditioned? Yes.
Is Nibbāna a refuge, a shelter, a resort, a final goal, the imperishable, the deathless?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Is dependent origination unconditioned, and Nibbāna unconditioned?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are there two unconditioned things?
One should not say so …pe…
"Are there two unconditioned things?
"Yes.
"Are they two refuges, two shelters, two resorts, two final goals, two states of immortality, two states of deathlessness, two nibbānas?"
It should not be said thus … [as before] … that there are two nibbānas? Yes.
Is there a high or low state, an inferior or superior state, a distinction or difference, a boundary or division, or a line or interval between the two kinds of Nibbāna?
One should not say so... [etc. ...
Is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) unconditioned (asaṅkhata)?
“Yes.
“Then is ignorance unconditioned?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is ignorance conditioned? Yes.
Is dependent origination conditioned?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is dependent origination unconditioned? Yes.
Are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance unconditioned?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance conditioned?
“Yes.
“Is dependent origination conditioned?
“One should not say so. … [as before] …
Is dependent origination unconditioned?
Yes. Is consciousness conditioned by formations unconditioned? No.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is consciousness conditioned by formations conditioned? Yes.
Is dependent origination conditioned?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is dependent origination unconditioned?
“Yes.
“Is it then the case that name-and-form conditioned by consciousness is unconditioned?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness?
Yes. Is dependent origination conditioned? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is dependent origination unconditioned? Yes.
Is aging-and-death conditioned by birth unconditioned?
One should not say so... [as before] ...
Is aging-and-death conditioned by birth conditioned?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) conditioned (saṅkhata)?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Should it not be said that "dependent origination is unconditioned"?
Yes, it should.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, with birth as condition there is aging-and-death.
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, specific conditionality."
The Tathāgata fully awakens to this and fully realizes it.
Having fully awakened to it and fully realized it, he declares it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.
And he says: "Behold!"
“With birth as condition, monks, there is aging and death.
With existence as condition, monks, there is birth...
[and so on] ...with ignorance as condition, monks, there are volitional formations.”
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, that element remains fixed...
[as before] ...and he says, "Behold":
"Conditioned by ignorance, monks, are volitional formations."
“Thus, monks, that which there is as suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness,
and specific conditionality— this, monks, is called dependent origination.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes, [it is].
In that case, dependent origination is unconditioned.

Is that which is the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā) and the fixed order of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatā) therein—expressed as “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”—unconditioned? Is Nibbāna unconditioned?
“Yes,” you say.
“Are there two unconditioned phenomena?
You should not speak thus … [as before] …
Are there two unconditioned things?
Yes. Are there two refuges? ... [and so on] ...
“Does the intermediate space blow?”—
one should not say so… [as before]… Is that which is the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā),

the fixed order of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatā), the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) therein, in the case of “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and that which is the stability of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, the unconditioned therein, in the case of “with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises”— is Nibbāna the unconditioned?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are there three unconditioned things?
One should not speak thus … [and so on] … No.
Are there three unconditioned things?
Yes. Are there three refuges? ... [and so on] ... Yes.
“Does the intermediate space blow?
One should not say so … [as before] … “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”:

that herein which is the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena, the unconditioned; “with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises”: that herein which is the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena, the unconditioned … [as before] …

“Is that which is the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā), the fixed order of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatā), the unconditioned therein—namely, ‘with birth as condition, aging-and-death arises’—the unconditioned Nibbāna?
Yes. “Are there twelve unconditioned things? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … that there are twelve unconditioned things? Yes.
"Are there twelve refuges and twelve shelters? ... [as before] ...
Does the intermediate space blow?
One must not say so... [as before]."
The Discussion on Dependent Origination is finished.
